title: Jansenius: indifference is not of the essence of freedom; freedom is the agent's mastery of itself
source_text: XXX. Si quidem ad communem libertatis rationem, & propriam ejus essentiam, pertinere non existimat voluntatis quandam indifferentiam, & indeterminationem respectu actus qui liber dicitur, per quam voluntas possit contrarium agere, aut saltem actum illum omittere, vel suspendere. Quippe ex ejus mente, libertas solum in eo consistit, quod agens liberum sibi & actui suo dominetur, & seipsum agat & moveat, non autem ab alio agatur & moveatur, quod locum habere contendit etiam in iis actibus, ad quos voluntas determinata est necessario & immutabiliter.
pass_a_gloss: For he does not think that to the common character of liberty, and its proper essence, there pertains a certain indifference and indetermination of the will in respect of the act which is called free, by which the will can do the contrary, or at least omit or suspend that act. For in his mind, liberty consists only in this, that the free agent is master of itself and of its act, and acts and moves itself, but is not acted on and moved by another, which he contends holds place even in those acts to which the will is determined necessarily and immutably.
pass_b_english: He does not hold that the general character and proper essence of freedom includes any indifference or indeterminacy of the will toward the act called free, such that the will could do the opposite, or at least leave the act undone or hold it back.

In his view freedom consists only in this: the free agent rules itself and its act, and it acts and moves itself rather than being acted on and moved by another. He maintains that this holds even in acts to which the will is fixed necessarily and unchangeably.

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
